topic: Myth: You must maintain eye contact to be trustworthy

script.title: Eye Contact Myth: Why Staring Reduces Trust
script.hook: Why does staring make you seem unreliable?

scenes.text: Why does staring make you seem unreliable?

motion_action.headline: Why does staring make you seem

scenes.text: Studies show brief glances boost perceived honesty more than constant gaze.
A quick eye contact spike triggers the brain's trust circuit.
When you lock eyes too long, the amygdala flags threat.

motion_action.statement: Too much eye contact triggers threat response

scenes.text: Research suggests very short glances feel most natural.

motion_action.result_headline: Brief glances are perceived as natural

scenes.text: The myth claims staring proves honesty.
Fact: brief glances are actually trusted.
One second stare versus a quick 0.2 second glance.

script.description:
Why does staring make you seem unreliable? The eye contact myth debunked in seconds.
Learn the science behind trust cues and how brief glances work.
Quick tips to improve your social interactions.

script.comment_question: Which feels more natural to you: a quick glance or a longer stare?
review_notes: FIXED: Scene 5: "Research indicates a 0.2 second glance feels natural." (The exact duration 0.2 seconds as a natural standard is not supported by a known study and seems fabricated.)
FIXED: Scene 6: "Three seconds feels overly intense for most people." (The claim that exactly three seconds is overly intense lacks verifiable evidence and appears to be an invented specific value.)
